item.title: Thoracic Paraspinal MFR — Broad, Sustained Contact
clinicalUse: A person says their upper back 'feels like cardboard' when twisting to reach the back seat. You check thoracic rotation and rib sensitivity rather than assuming fascia is adhered.
A slow, tolerable soft-tissue contact may be used as a short adjunct when it helps comfortable movement, not as proof of tissue remodelling.
Compare the same seated thoracic rotation and breathing comfort after the trial.
patientPosition: Prone with the head and rib cage supported, or side-lying if prone is uncomfortable or affects breathing.
Allow the shoulder girdle to relax and ensure no pressure restricts respiration.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the upper/mid-thoracic region with a stable base; contact is broad enough to avoid digging at one rib.
Maintain relaxed wrists and shift body weight gently rather than pressing with stiff thumbs.
stabilization: Support chest and head in a neutral comfortable line; ask the patient to breathe normally during contact.
Stabilize with broad gentle contact rather than forced thoracic extension.
contact: Use palms or a supported cross-hand contact across the paraspinal/inter-scapular muscular region, lateral to the spinous processes.
Avoid direct focused pressure over spinous processes, ribs that may be injured, or vulnerable medical/surgical sites.
forceDirection: For direct work, slowly take up the perceived soft-tissue slack with gentle opposing hand vectors over a broad area.
For indirect work, follow an easier direction and wait without adding sudden thrust or painful stretch.
dosage: A gentle sustained contact for about 30–90 seconds can be a training example, with regular checks for comfort and breathing.
There is no established optimal duration for fascial tissue change; retest rather than treating until an imagined release occurs.
steps: Measure the original seated thoracic rotation or comfortable upper-back reach before treatment.
Screen trauma, rib fracture concern, unexplained chest pain, infection, osteoporosis-related vulnerability and neurological red flags.
Support the chest and head comfortably in prone or side-lying while preserving easy breathing.
Place broad contacts lateral to the spinous processes across a suitable paraspinal muscular region.
Apply slow, low-force sustained load toward comfortable resistance or ease, using the selected direct/indirect approach.
Monitor breathing and guarding; stop or reduce pressure if symptoms become unpleasant or spread.
Return contact to neutral, repeat the target rotation, then practise controlled active thoracic mobility if helpful.
reassess: Seated thoracic rotation and back-seat reach
mistakes: Treating a rib or vertebral spinous process like a muscle belly.
Pressing harder when the patient holds their breath.
Explaining a short-lived movement change as proof that fascia melted.
safety: Unexplained chest pain, dyspnea or serious cardiopulmonary symptoms warrant medical evaluation rather than manual therapy.
Avoid suspected rib fracture, infection, recent unstable surgery or significant bone fragility.
Stop for new neurological symptoms, marked chest discomfort or difficulty breathing during positioning.
item.visualCue: Broad sustained paraspinal contact, breathing freely → retest seated upper-back rotation.

story.title: The upper back that thinks it's cardboard
story.scene: Someone turns toward the back seat and stops halfway. 'My upper back feels like cardboard.' The clinician notices the rotation restriction, but before manual contact checks whether chest, rib or neurological warning signs make the situation inappropriate.
story.clinicalDecision: The rib cage and head are supported. Broad, slow contact sits beside the thoracic spine, not on an irritated rib. The patient keeps breathing normally while the clinician explores a comfortable direct or indirect myofascial load.
story.retest: Seated rotation is measured again. A small improvement can become an opportunity for active thoracic mobility; it does not prove the fascia was melted, folded or ironed.
story.punchline: Cardboard belongs in packaging, not in a diagnostic label.
story.evidenceCaveat: Contemporary reviews discuss multiple potential manual-therapy mechanisms. The specific structural explanations commonly attached to MFR remain uncertain.
